prf:aether-parameter-exists:
Proof Proof of existence of the aether parameter. The braiding c_{V,V} \colon V \otimes V \to V \otimes V of the QOU provides the aether parameter categorically — no external choice is needed.

Step 1 (spectral decomposition). The volume constraint \epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \twoheadrightarrow \mathbf{1} splits V \otimes V = S^2 V \oplus \Lambda^2 V into eigenspaces of c_{V,V}. Since \Lambda^2 V \cong \mathbf{1} is simple and \dim S^2 V = 3, the braiding acts by scalars \lambda_+ \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) on S^2 V and \lambda_- \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) on \Lambda^2 V.

Step 2 (define q). Set q := \lambda_+. The determinant constraint \lambda_+ \cdot \lambda_- = -1 (from \det(c_{V,V}) = -1 on a rank-2 object with trivial determinant) forces \lambda_- = -q^{-1}. Therefore c_{V,V} satisfies the Hecke relation (T - q)(T + q^{-1}) = 0 (braiding eigenvalue extraction).

Step 3 (non-degeneracy). The QOU assumption c_{V,V}^2 \neq \mathrm{id} ensures q \neq \pm 1. The positive-definite dagger structure forces q \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}, and the non-root-of-unity condition q \notin \mu_\infty(k) follows from transcendence over \mathbb{Q} in the archimedean realisation.

Step 4 (agreement with d_q). The categorical q extracted from the braiding coincides with the interpolation parameter in d_q = q^{-1}d + (1 - q^{-1})\pi_V \circ d: both are characterised as the unique q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) for which the Iwahori--Hecke algebra H_n(q) acts faithfully on V^{\otimes n}.

In the archimedean realisation, the constant aether field q(p) = q_0 > 1 for all p satisfies the classicality bound q \ge 1 and positivity. Non-constant aether fields arise from the Reeb flow parameterisation of the categorical \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})-valued coordinate.
thm:aether-parameter-unique: Theorem Uniqueness of the aether parameter. Given a QOU (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau), the aether parameter q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) is uniquely determined as a parameter: the braiding spectrum and the positive-definite dagger select exactly one scalar from the Hecke eigenvalue pair \{q, -q^{-1}\} (the positive one). This is parameter uniqueness — the extraction procedure is canonical, with no ambiguity or choice. It does not mean q takes a single value. The aether parameter is a field q \colon M \to \mathbb{R}_{>0} that varies across the manifold and with energy scale; high-energy processes see a different q than low-energy ones. The observed value q_0 at the location and energy of observation is empirical.
prf:aether-parameter-unique:
Proof Proof of uniqueness of the aether parameter. Suppose q, q' \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) are both aether parameters for the same QOU (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau). Each extracts from the same braiding c_{V,V} via the spectral decomposition of existence.

Step 1 (spectral data is intrinsic). The rigid monoidal structure and the volume constraint \epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \twoheadrightarrow \mathbf{1} determine the canonical splitting V \otimes V = S^2 V \oplus \Lambda^2 V uniquely as the eigenspace decomposition of c_{V,V} under the induced H_2(q)-action (the braiding generates the two-strand Iwahori--Hecke algebra, the q-deformation of S_2); neither summand involves a choice. Hence the eigenvalues \lambda_+, \lambda_- \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) of c_{V,V} on S^2 V and \Lambda^2 V are intrinsic invariants.

Step 2 (Hecke relation pins eigenvalue pair). By braiding eigenvalue extraction, c_{V,V} satisfies (T - \lambda_+)(T - \lambda_-) = 0 with \lambda_+ \lambda_- = -1. Thus the unordered pair \{\lambda_+, \lambda_-\} = \{q, -q^{-1}\} is determined by the QOU, so q \in \{\lambda_+, -\lambda_-^{-1}\}, and the same for q'.

Step 3 (positivity pins the sign). The positive-definite dagger structure induced by (\int_A, S) forces q \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}: the q-eigenvalue of the symmetric braiding channel must be strictly positive because \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_q = \int_A \circ \mu \circ (S \otimes c_{V,V}) is positive definite only when the S^2 V-eigenvalue is positive. The same constraint applies to q'.

Step 4 (conclusion). From Step 2, q, q' \in \{\lambda_+, -\lambda_-^{-1}\}; from Step 3 both are positive. Since \lambda_+ > 0 and -\lambda_-^{-1} = q (from \lambda_+ \lambda_- = -1), the two candidates coincide: q = q' = \lambda_+. In the archimedean realisation, the same argument applies pointwise on M, so the aether field q \colon M \to \mathbb{R}_{>0} is uniquely determined by the QOU data. \square
ex:aether-parameter-su2: Example Aether parameter for \mathrm{SU}(2). For \mathrm{SU}(2), the algebraic parameter q is realized by a ring homomorphism \iota(q) = q_0 \in \mathbb{C}^\times. Setting q_0 = 1 recovers the classical commutative ring \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). Setting q_0 = e^{\pi i / \kappa} produces the non-commutative relations ab = q_0 ba, etc., leaving a finite semisimple category where quantum dimensions take the form [2j+1]_{q_0}. The parameter interpolates between the classical gauge theory and a topological quantum field theory.
ex:aether-parameter-brings: Example Constructive extraction of q on Bring's surface. On Bring's surface, V \otimes V \cong V_1 \oplus V_0. The R-matrix eigenvalues are q and -q^{-1}. By the Hecke relation the unordered pair \{q, -q^{-1}\} is intrinsic; the positive-definite dagger selects q > 0. The categorical parameter q is a real-valued function on M: at each point p \in M the braiding spectrum extracts a local q(p) \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}. The observed aether parameter q_0 at the point of observation is an empirical value, not derived from the topology of Bring's surface; the Euler characteristic \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = -6 constrains the quantum dimension [2]_q but does \emph{not} fix the pointwise value of q_0.
sec:quantum-universe-explication:
Deformation parameter and quantum gauge group.

The aether parameter q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) characterizes the \mathbb{G}_m-family of interpolations between the full differential d and the vertical projection \pi_V \circ d. Fixing q deforms the categorical dimension of the fundamental object from 2 to [2]_q = q + q^{-1}, and the gauge group from \mathrm{SU}(2) to \mathrm{SU}_q(2). Every subsequent physical feature—commutators, Reeb derivations, and action traces—is governed strictly by this single categorical parameter.
def:quantum-gauge-group:
Definition Quantum Gauge Group. The reconstructed Hopf algebra H = \mathrm{End}^{\otimes}(\tau) gives the quantum gauge group G_q = \mathrm{SU}_q(2), with q categorically fixed by the symmetric braiding eigenvalue.

Here H is the coend \int^{X \in \mathbf{C}} \tau(X)^{\vee} \otimes_R \tau(X) = \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)), whose dual is \mathrm{End}^{\otimes}(\tau). The group of points \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)(R) is the set of characters H \to R under convolution. When q^2 - 1 is invertible in R, every character is diagonal, (\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta) \mapsto (u, 0, 0, u^{-1}) with u \in R^{\times}, so \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)(R) \cong R^{\times} is the maximal torus (Lean: QOU.AlgebraicSubstrate.OqSU2.charEquivUnits). Away from the symmetric point, G_q is therefore the Hopf algebra H and not a group of points, and the map \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \to G is the inclusion of the maximal torus. The identification \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2) is classical Tannaka duality at q = 1, where the algebra is commutative and has non-diagonal characters (exists_nondiag_char_at_one). The Haar state is invariant under translation by every character (haarState_rightTrans_char, haarState_leftTrans_char).

The modular automorphism is a point of \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau). Write \chi_u for the diagonal character and \star for convolution. Left translation by \chi_u followed by right translation by \chi_v sends (\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta) to (uv\,\alpha,\ uv^{-1}\beta,\ u^{-1}v\,\gamma,\ u^{-1}v^{-1}\delta). At u = v = q^{-1} this is the modular automorphism \sigma = (q^{-2}\alpha, \beta, \gamma, q^{2}\delta) of the Haar state, so

  \sigma(x) = \chi_{q^{-1}} \star x \star \chi_{q^{-1}}, \qquad h(xy) = h(y\,\sigma(x))

(Lean: modularAut_eq_twoSided, haarState_modular). The twist of the Haar trace is therefore the pivotal point \chi_{q^{-1}} of \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) acting on both sides. It is not a conjugation, since conjugation \chi \star x \star \chi^{-1} preserves h and would give an untwisted trace. Haar itself is fixed by every one-sided translation: h(\chi \star x) = h(x \star \chi) = h(x).
rem:quantum-gauge-group-remark: Remark The quantum gauge group as a local field. Over a spacetime M, the quantum gauge group defines a local field of quantum groups \{G_{q(p)}\}_{p \in M}.
ex:su2-characters-and-quantum-dimension:
Example \mathrm{SU}(2) characters, and the quantum dimension as one evaluation of them. Continuing \mathrm{SU}(2) as a quantum universe, the simple objects are the irreducible representations V_n, n \geq 0, of dimension n + 1; the Grothendieck group is \mathbb{Z}[x] with x = [V_1].

Characters. Restricted to the maximal torus \{ \mathrm{diag}(t, t^{-1}) \}, the weights of V_n are n, n-2, \dots, -n, so its character is the Laurent polynomial

  \mathrm{ch}(V_n)(t) \;=\; t^{n} + t^{n-2} + \cdots + t^{-n} \;=\; t^{-n}\bigl(1 + t^{2} + \cdots + t^{2n}\bigr).

Characters are additive on direct sums and multiplicative on tensor products, and a representation of \mathrm{SU}(2) is determined by its character; so [V] \mapsto \mathrm{ch}(V) identifies K_0(\mathrm{Rep}\,\mathrm{SU}(2)) with the ring \mathbb{Z}[t, t^{-1}]^{S_2} of Laurent polynomials symmetric under t \mapsto t^{-1} [fulton-harris1991]. This is the Chern character of the category in the presentation of HH_0 by class functions: the class [\mathrm{id}_{V_n}] corresponds to the function \mathrm{ch}(V_n) on the torus.

Two evaluations. At t = 1 every term is 1, and \mathrm{ch}(V_n)(1) = n + 1 = \dim V_n. At t = q, the quantum group \mathrm{SU}_q(2) has the same simple objects and the same characters, but its rigid trace is the quantum trace, weighted by the pivotal element; the quantum dimension is the character evaluated there,

  \dim_q(V_n) \;=\; \mathrm{ch}(V_n)(q) \;=\; \frac{q^{n+1} - q^{-(n+1)}}{q - q^{-1}} \;=\; [n+1]_q ,

the symmetric quantum integer [kassel1995]. For the fundamental object, \dim_q(V_1) = q + q^{-1} = [2]_q. Three identities carry the example: \mathrm{ch}(V_n)(1) = n+1, (q - q^{-1})\,\mathrm{ch}(V_n)(q) = q^{n+1} - q^{-(n+1)}, and \mathrm{ch}(V_1)(q) = q + q^{-1}.

What the example shows. The character has n + 1 terms and does not depend on q; the quantum dimension is a single number and does. Their relation is exactly \dim_q = \mathrm{ev}_q \circ \mathrm{ch} of the definition, with \mathrm{ev}_q the evaluation of a class function at the pivotal element. Two consequences follow at once. First, \dim_q(V_n) > 0 for every real q > 0 and every n: a quantum dimension in this category is positive, and a negative number such as -6 cannot be one. Second, for the coordinate algebra A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) the Peter–Weyl decomposition [A] = \sum_{n \geq 0} (n+1)[V_n] lives in a completion of K_0, and its quantum dimension \sum_{n \geq 0} (n+1)[n+1]_q — or \sum_m [m]_q^{2} for A as a bimodule — is a divergent series at every real q \neq 1; what one assigns to it is a matter of regularisation, taken up where the base curve is discussed.
def:quantum-planck-constant: Definition Quantum Planck Constant. The quantum Planck constant is defined as \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}.
rem:planck-limits: Remark Limiting regimes of \hbar_q. As q \to 1, \hbar_q \to 0 and quantum effects vanish. As q \to \infty, \hbar_q \to 1.
def:q-hodge-star:
Definition q-Hodge star. The q-Hodge star is the deformed involution \star_q \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{n-k}(A), defined by:

  \alpha \wedge_q \star_q \beta
  =  q \cdot \int_A\!\bigl(\alpha^* \cdot \beta\bigr) \mathrm{vol}.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q-hodge-star-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "\star_q"] \ar[d, "\star"']
  & \Omega^{n-k}(A) \\
  \Omega^{n-k}(A) \ar[ur, "q \cdot \mathrm{id}"']
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
rem:q-hodge-star-remark: Remark The factor q in the q-Hodge star. The extra factor q in the q-Hodge star scales the inner product, coupling Hodge duality directly to the deformation.
def:exceptional-divisor: Definition Exceptional divisor at p. Let p \in M be a brane point with normal N and tangent frame (T_1, T_2). The blow-up map replaces p with the exceptional divisor \mathcal{S}_p \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}), defined by the geometric locus of scaled tangent vectors parameterized by angles \phi, \psi.
def:commutative-qou: Definition Strictly commutative QOU (commutative specialisation). A quantum observable universe is strictly commutative if its multiplication and comultiplication are respectively commutative and cocommutative.
rem:commutative-qou-remark: Remark The strictly commutative case as the classical limit. Strict commutativity isolates the classical limit q \to 1: it restricts the gauge group to \mathrm{SU}(2) and turns \mathrm{Rep}(\mathbf{C}) into a symmetric category. A strictly commutative quantum observable universe hosts the classical hyperelliptic quintic, but cannot support anyonic structure.
prop:u1-equivariant-reduction: Proposition \mathrm{U}(1)-equivariant reduction of the exceptional divisor. On the exceptional divisor \mathcal{S}_p, restricting observables to those equivariant under the \mathrm{U}(1) polar rotation yields the orbit space \mathcal{S}_p / \mathrm{U}(1) \cong [0, \pi]. Over the interior, this simplifies the observable algebra to a free \mathrm{U}(1)-bundle parameterized by a single phase.
prf:u1-equivariant-reduction:
Proof Proof of u1 equivariant reduction. Sketch. Using the spherical parametrisation of def:exceptional-divisor, the \mathrm{U}(1) action is \psi \mapsto \psi + \alpha, leaving \phi fixed. Quotienting by \psi identifies orbits with \phi \in [0,\pi]; the two fixed points \phi = 0, \pi (the poles) collapse the \psi fibre to a point, while over \phi \in (0, \pi) the fibre is isomorphic to S^1 with phase coordinate \psi. \mathrm{U}(1)-equivariant observables therefore descend to sections of the associated phase-S^1 bundle over (0, \pi), which in the commutative limit is trivialisable to give a single global phase coordinate \varphi \in S^1. \square

Scope of the claim. The statement does not say the geometric fibre \mathcal{S}_p itself collapses --- it remains \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) \cong S^2. What collapses is the \mathrm{U}(1)-invariant observable algebra, which reduces to functions on S^1 modulo the two polar fixed points. The physical interpretation of this S^1 as the single \mathrm{U}(1) phase tube is taken up in the chapter on nuclear interactions and binding.
prop:quantum-observable-universe-exists: Proposition Existence of quantum observable universes. Given a principal \mathrm{SU}(2)-bundle over a compact oriented manifold satisfying the measurability condition c_1 = c_2 = 0, there exists a quantum observable universe. Setting \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{Rep}(U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)), A = \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)), and \tau to the forgetful functor realizes the axioms explicitly.
lem:qou-exists-axiom-1: Lemma Axiom 1 — Haar state gives a non-degenerate Frobenius pairing. The Haar state on \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)) provides the faithful integration.
prf:qou-exists-axiom-1: Proof Proof of axiom 1 (Frobenius pairing) for QOU existence. The Haar state h = \int_{A} is faithful: for any non-zero a \in A there exists b \in A with h(ab) \neq 0. This is the content of Woronowicz's reconstruction theorem [woronowicz1987]. Faithfulness is equivalent to non-degeneracy of (a, b) \mapsto h(ab), which yields the isomorphism A \xrightarrow{\sim} A^{\vee} required by axiom~(1). \square
lem:qou-exists-axiom-2: Lemma Axiom 2 — the adjoint representation of \mathfrak{sl}_2 has no invariants. For \mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{sl}_2 over a field of characteristic \neq 2, the adjoint representation is the irreducible spin-1 representation V_1, and \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, V_1) = 0. The statement concerns the adjoint representation of the Lie algebra (or of U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2) at generic q), not the adjoint coaction of \mathcal{O}_q(G) on itself, whose invariants are nonzero.
prf:qou-exists-axiom-2:
Proof Proof of axiom 2 (observability) for QOU existence. Take \mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{sl}_2. Its adjoint representation is three-dimensional with weights 2, 0, -2 for the Cartan element H, so it is the irreducible highest-weight module V_1 of highest weight 2 (spin 1). At generic q the finite-dimensional type-1 modules of U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2) are classified by the same highest weights, and V_1 stays simple [kassel1995]. The unit object \mathbf{1} is the one-dimensional module of highest weight 0. Two simple modules with different highest weights are not isomorphic, so by Schur's lemma \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, V_1) = 0. \square

The claim concerns the adjoint representation of the Lie algebra (or of U_q(\mathfrak{g})), not the adjoint coaction of \mathcal{O}_q(G) on itself. By the Peter--Weyl decomposition \mathcal{O}_q(G) \cong \bigoplus_{\lambda} V_\lambda^{*} \otimes V_\lambda [woronowicz1988], each summand V_\lambda^{*} \otimes V_\lambda \cong \mathrm{End}(V_\lambda) carries the invariant \mathrm{id}_{V_\lambda}, so the invariants of that coaction are the class functions, one for each \lambda, and are not zero modulo the unit. The previous version of this proof argued the opposite.
lem:qou-exists-axiom-3:
Lemma Axiom 3 — Vanishing categorical Chern classes for the adjoint bundle.

Under the structural hypothesis that the classical principal bundle P satisfies c_1(\mathrm{Ad}(P)) = c_2(\mathrm{Ad}(P)) = 0, the corresponding categorical Chern classes of the adjoint bundle in the quantum observable universe must also vanish:

  c_i(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) := c_i(\tau(\mathrm{Ad}(A))) = 0 \quad \text{for } i \in \{1, 2\}.

It ensures that the categorical formulation is free of the standard topological obstructions that would otherwise manifest as anomalies. In the event that c_2(\mathrm{Ad}(P)) \neq 0, one replaces the base category with the modular tensor category \mathbf{Rep}_k(\widehat{\mathfrak{g}}) at level k = \langle c_2, [M] \rangle, thereby absorbing the non-vanishing anomaly into the ribbon twist.
prf:qou-exists-axiom-3:
Proof Proof of axiom 3 (Chern classes) for QOU existence. Categorical Chern classes are defined via \tau: c_{i}(X) := c_{i}(\tau(X)). For X = \mathrm{Ad}(A) with archimedean realisation \tau(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = \mathrm{Ad}(P), these are the Chern classes of the adjoint bundle of P, and the proposition's hypothesis c_{1}(\mathrm{Ad}(P)) = c_{2}(\mathrm{Ad}(P)) = 0 is exactly axiom~(3).

For c_{2}(\mathrm{Ad}(P)) \neq 0 one replaces \mathbf{C} by the modular tensor category \mathbf{Rep}_{k}(\widehat{\mathfrak{g}}) at level k = \langle c_{2}, [M] \rangle, obtained by quotienting the tilting modules of U_{q}(\mathfrak{g}) at q = e^{\pi i/(k + h^{\vee})} by the negligible ideal [reshetikhin1991]. The Chern--Simons level is then absorbed into the ribbon twist, and the axiom is replaced by compatibility with the CS level. Under the present hypothesis c_{2} = 0 reduces to k = 0, and generic q suffices. \square
lem:qou-exists-axiom-4: Lemma Axiom 4 — categorical volume constraint via the quantum determinant. The standard determinant on V \cong \mathbb{C}^2 satisfies the volume constraint.
prf:qou-exists-axiom-4:
Proof Proof of axiom 4 (volume constraint) for QOU existence. Let V \in \mathbf{C} be the standard representation (dimension n = \dim V_{\mathrm{std}}). The top exterior power \Lambda^{n} V is the 1-dimensional trivial module, \Lambda^{n} V \cong \mathbf{1}, with isomorphism \epsilon \colon \Lambda^{n} V \to \mathbf{1} given by the q-deformed determinant (the quantum volume form) [kassel1995]. By G-invariance of the determinant,

  \epsilon \circ \Lambda^{n}(g_{V})
  \;=\;
  g_{\mathbf{1}} \circ \epsilon
  \;=\; \epsilon
  \quad \text{for all } g \in \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau),

which is axiom~(4). \square
prf:quantum-observable-universe-exists:
Proof Proof of existence of quantum observable universes. The triple (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) is exhibited below, together with a check of the four axioms of quantum observable universe.

Construction

For q \in \mathbb{C}^{\times} not a non-trivial root of unity, take \mathbf{C} := \mathbf{Rep}(U_{q}(\mathfrak{g})) — the rigid ribbon braided monoidal category of finite-dimensional type-I representations of the Drinfeld--Jimbo quantum group [chari1994guide, kassel1995]; A := \mathcal{O}_{q}(G) — the restricted dual Hopf algebra of matrix coefficients [woronowicz1988, chari1994guide], with \int_{A} := h the unique faithful invariant Haar state [woronowicz1987]; and \tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to \mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}} the (faithful) forgetful functor.

Verification of axioms

The four axioms hold by (axiom 1: Frobenius pairing), (axiom 2: observability), (axiom 3: Chern classes), and (axiom 4: volume constraint) respectively.

Conclusion

All four axioms hold for (\mathbf{Rep}(U_{q}(\mathfrak{g})), \mathcal{O}_{q}(G), \mathrm{forget}) under the Chern-class hypothesis, establishing existence. The triple specialises to the archimedean realisation (the \mathbb{C}-QOU example later in this chapter) upon choosing a fibre functor landing in a module category over a contact CR manifold.

Non-uniqueness. Any (\mathbf{C}', A', \tau') with \mathbf{C}' Morita-equivalent to \mathbf{Rep}(U_{q}(\mathfrak{g})) and A' Hopf-equivalent to \mathcal{O}_{q}(G) gives another QOU. Uniqueness up to such equivalences is Tannaka--Krein reconstruction [woronowicz1988], taken here as background and not re-proved. \square
prose:intro-heisenberg-commutator: The Heisenberg commutator [\hat{p}, \hat{q}] = -i\hbar emerges from the fibre structure of \mathcal{S} rather than as a postulated relation. This section proves the aether Heisenberg commutator as a structural identity and exhibit the non-commutative drag that the categorical commutator imparts on the geometry.
def:q-deformed-commutator:
Definition q-deformed commutator [\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q. Let \hat{X}, \hat{P} be the position and momentum observables on the fibre \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}). Let J \colon H \to H be the complex structure on the Levi distribution (J^2 = -\mathrm{Id}). Let q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) be the aether parameter. The q-deformed commutator of \hat{X} and \hat{P} at a point p \in M is

  [\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q := J\,\hbar_q(p),
  \qquad \hbar_q(p) = 1 - q(p)^{-1},

where \hbar_q is the quantum Planck constant.
prop:heisenberg-commutator:
Proposition q-deformed Heisenberg commutator from the Reeb fibre. Let [\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q = J\hbar_q(p) be the q-deformed commutator of the fibre observables \hat{X}, \hat{P} on \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}). The commutator interpolates between the classical and maximally-uncertain regimes:

  1. As q \to 1, [\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q \to 0 (classical limit, \hbar_q \to 0).
  2. As q \to \infty, [\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q \to J (maximal uncertainty, \hbar_q \to 1).
rem:heisenberg-commutator:
Remark Heisenberg commutator and the Reeb fibre. The Heisenberg uncertainty principle emerges as a fibre coordinate measurement. The q-deformed commutator measures displacement along the Reeb fibre. The complex structure J \colon H \to H on the Levi distribution supplies the imaginary unit, and the quantum Planck constant \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1} measures the displacement itself. The aether parameter q parametrises the categorical interpolation family.

As q \to 1, the observer sits at the base of the Reeb fibre, where d_q = d, and [\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q \to 0. As q \to \infty, the observer sits at the tip of the fibre, where d_q \to \pi_V \circ d, and [\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q \to J.

Geometrically, [\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q equals \varTheta(\xi_q), the q-deformed Reeb field evaluated on the contact form. The field \xi_q is the unique direction along which d\varTheta degenerates, encoding the obstruction to commutativity. The observer's position in the fibre determines how much the observables fail to commute.
sec:algebraic-layer-intro:
The algebraic layer is the Frobenius--Hopf algebra A viewed as a graded ring equipped with the Reeb derivation—the differential operator forced by the categorical volume constraint. The algebraic programme runs as follows: aether structure and Reeb derivation, the unit particle as a categorical invariant, spectral trace and Tannaka--Krein duality, geometric stability via the Hasse--Weil bound, and the classical limit recovering the macroscopic continuum.

The spectral trace formula relates the q-zeta function of A to the Chebyshev function of the Reeb flow. A stability criterion derives from the Weil bound on the fibre geometry. The classical limit q \to 1 emerges as a functor that fails to be an equivalence, with the obstruction to classicality acting as a non-trivial categorical invariant.
sec:algebraic-layer-preamble:
This section exhibits the algebraic object whose internal geometry generates the physical observations. The quantum vacuum formalises as a self-dual Frobenius--Hopf algebra A living in a rigid monoidal category \mathbf{C}.

The algebra A carries three layers of structure. The Frobenius form \lambda \colon A \to \mathbf{1} and the Hopf comultiplication \Delta \colon A \to A \otimes A endow A with an inner product and a coalgebra structure, related by the Frobenius compatibility condition. A categorical Reeb derivation \xi_q \colon A \to A encodes the observer drift—the intrinsic time evolution generated by the contact structure on the state bundle \mathcal{S}. The spectral geometry of Bring's curve \mathcal{B} provides the coordinate fibers: the 2g = 8 independent cycles of this genus-4 curve determine the fundamental modes of the Reeb spectrum.

Self-duality is the principle that closes the construction. The rigid dualizing complex \omega_A^\bullet forms the duality theory for the non-commutative algebra A [yekutieli2010]. The Frobenius form induces a quasi-isomorphism A \xrightarrow{\sim} \omega_A^\bullet, establishing that the observer trace \Phi = \lambda \circ \mu and the observed state space are intrinsically paired. The aether is simultaneously the algebra of observables and the space on which those observables act.

Algebraic and geometric precedent on \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)). Two structural distinctions separate the infinite-dimensional coordinate algebra \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)) from the finite-rank Frobenius towers used later in this paper. By the theorem of Richard G. Larson and Moss E. Sweedler [larson-sweedler1969], every finite-dimensional Hopf algebra over a field carries a Frobenius form supplied by a nonzero integral; conversely, Bertrand I-peng Lin [lin1977] proved that an infinite-dimensional coalgebra or Hopf algebra admits no nonzero integral of finite dual rank, so \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)) as a whole is not a unital Frobenius algebra. Infinite-dimensional group and quantum-group coordinate algebras instead form multiplier Hopf algebras in the sense of Alfons Van Daele [vandaele1994], or nonunital and H^*-Frobenius structures in the infinite-dimensional categorical quantum mechanics of Samson Abramsky and Chris Heunen [abramsky-heunen2012]. In this paper, genuine Frobenius objects enter only at finite rank: either on finite-dimensional truncations or along the finite-level Iwahori--Hecke and Temperley--Lieb centralizer tower, which forms a tower of Frobenius extensions in the sense of Lars Kadison [kadison1999] whose convention-D Markov trace has subfactor index [2]_q^2 \ge 4 in the positive range of Vaughan F. R. Jones [jones1983]. Moreover, on \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)) at q \neq \pm 1, the Haar state constructed by Stanisław Lech Woronowicz [woronowicz1987] is non-tracial and carries a nontrivial modular automorphism \vartheta satisfying h(ab) = h(b\,\vartheta(a)); that modular automorphism of the coordinate algebra is not the Nakayama twist of the finite Iwahori--Hecke / Temperley--Lieb tower, where the Markov trace on the semisimple Temperley--Lieb quotient is symmetric (\mathrm{tr}_M(xy) = \mathrm{tr}_M(yx)) and the tower therefore has trivial Nakayama automorphism \nu = \mathrm{id}.

The differential, bundle, and Hodge ingredients assembled on the \mathrm{SU}_q(2) model likewise rest on established noncommutative geometry. Woronowicz constructed the three-dimensional left-covariant differential calculus on \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)) [woronowicz1987-twisted-su2] and the general theory of bicovariant differential calculi on compact matrix pseudogroups [woronowicz1989], while Piotr Stachura [stachura1992] and Konrad Schmüdgen and Axel Schüler [schmudgen-schuler1995] classified the four-dimensional bicovariant calculi on \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)) and \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SL}(N)). Over the quantum two-spheres introduced by Piotr Podleś [podles1987], Tomasz Brzeziński and Shahn Majid [brzezinski-majid1993] developed quantum principal bundles and the q-monopole connection, Shahn Majid [majid1995, majid2002, majid2005] formulated braided and noncommutative Riemannian and spin geometry on the standard q-sphere, Réamonn Ó Buachalla [obuachalla2016] constructed noncommutative complex structures on quantum homogeneous spaces, Giovanni Landi and Alessandro Zampini [landi-zampini2011] studied differential calculi, Hodge operators, and Laplacians on the quantum Hopf fibration, and Partha Sarathi Chakraborty and Arupkumar Pal [chakraborty-pal2003] together with Ludwik Dąbrowski, Giovanni Landi, Andrzej Sitarz, Walter van Suijlekom, and Joseph C. Várilly [dabrowski-landi-sitarz-vansuijlekom-varilly2005] constructed equivariant spectral triples and the Dirac operator on \mathrm{SU}_q(2). No new differential calculus on \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)) is claimed here; the chapter organises the three-dimensional left-covariant contact and Reeb datum into the categorical action functional used downstream.
def:frobenius-hopf-aether:
Definition The quantum vacuum as a Frobenius--Hopf algebra. Let \mathbf{C} be a braided monoidal category, with braiding \beta. A Frobenius--Hopf aether is a sextuple (A, \mu, \eta, \Delta, \varepsilon, S) in \mathbf{C} equipped with a Frobenius form \lambda \colon A \to \mathbf{1} satisfying the following axioms:

  1. Algebra structure: The morphisms \mu \colon A \otimes A \to A and \eta \colon \mathbf{1} \to A make A an associative unital algebra object in \mathbf{C}.

  2. Coalgebra structure and antipode: The morphisms \Delta \colon A \to A \otimes A and \varepsilon \colon A \to \mathbf{1} make A a coassociative counital coalgebra object.

    The antipode S \colon A \to A is an involutive anti-automorphism of the whole structure:

\[
\begin{aligned}
  S \circ \mu &= \mu \circ \beta_{A,A} \circ (S \otimes S),
  &\qquad \Delta \circ S &= (S \otimes S) \circ \beta_{A,A} \circ \Delta, \\
  S \circ \eta &= \eta,
  &\qquad \varepsilon \circ S &= \varepsilon, \\
  S \circ S &= \mathrm{id}_A,
  &\qquad \lambda \circ S &= \lambda.
\end{aligned}
\]
  1. Frobenius relation: The Frobenius form \lambda satisfies \mu \circ \Delta = (\Delta \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \alpha \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \mu), where \alpha is the associator in \mathbf{C}.
  2. Non-degeneracy: Write \mathrm{ev} = \lambda \circ \mu \colon A \otimes A \to \mathbf{1} for the Frobenius pairing \langle a, b \rangle_F = \lambda(\mu(a \otimes b)). There is a morphism \mathrm{coev} \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \otimes A such that both snake identities hold:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathrm{id}_A \otimes \mathrm{ev}) \circ (\mathrm{coev} \otimes \mathrm{id}_A) &= \mathrm{id}_A, \\
(\mathrm{ev} \otimes \mathrm{id}_A) \circ (\mathrm{id}_A \otimes \mathrm{coev}) &= \mathrm{id}_A,
\end{aligned}
\]

each read modulo the unitors and the associator of \mathbf{C}.

  1. Self-duality: The pair (\mathrm{ev}, \mathrm{coev}) exhibits A as its own dual.
rem:frobenius-hopf-aether-remark:
Remark The counit, the antipode and self-duality of the aether. The counit. The counit of a Frobenius--Hopf aether is not required to be multiplicative: together with the Frobenius relation and counitality, \varepsilon(ab) = \varepsilon(a)\,\varepsilon(b) forces x = \varepsilon(x)\cdot 1 for every x, so A would be spanned by its unit.

The antipode. The braiding \beta is what makes "reverses" expressible, which is why \mathbf{C} is taken braided; that is no extra demand, since the aether is invoked at the level of a quantum universe, which is braided monoidal.

The antipode is constrained but not determined. Every classical unimodular antipode (such as S(g) = g^{-1} on k[G] or inversion on \mathcal{O}(G) at q = 1) satisfies the six conditions on S, and on a non-commutative A they exclude the trivial choice S = \mathrm{id}_A. Away from the involutive unimodular point --- for instance on \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)) at q \neq \pm 1, where S^2(\beta) = q^{-2}\beta, or on a non-unimodular finite Hopf algebra such as the Taft algebra H_4, where S^2(X) = -X and \lambda \circ S \neq \lambda --- the last two identities deform to the pivotal square law S \circ S = \gamma_A for an automorphism \gamma_A \colon A \xrightarrow{\sim} A and the modular-shifted law \lambda \circ S = \lambda \circ \mu_{\mathrm{mod}}. Even in the involutive case these conditions do not single S out: the only condition that does is the convolution identity \mu \circ (S \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \Delta = \eta \circ \varepsilon, and that identity forces A to be trivial whenever the scalars form a field, so it cannot be imposed here.

Self-duality. Self-duality couples the observer trace \Phi = \lambda \circ \mu to the observed state space intrinsically, and it is what makes the left and right categorical traces on \mathrm{End}(A) available.

Duals are required of A only, not of \mathbf{C}. The non-degeneracy axiom supplies \mathrm{coev} as part of the data, so A carries its own duality datum and no object of \mathbf{C} other than A need have a dual. Consequently a Frobenius--Hopf object is available already at the level of a quantum universe, which is braided monoidal but not rigid; rigidity is imposed one level up, on a quantum observable universe, where duals for every object carry the antiparticles and let a strand close into a knot.
def:brings-coordinate-ring:
Definition Non-commutative coordinate ring of Bring's curve. Bring's curve \mathcal{B} \subset \mathbb{P}^4 is the complete intersection

\mathcal{B}
=  V\!\bigl(
  \textstyle\sum x_i,
  \textstyle\sum x_i^2,
  \textstyle\sum x_i^3
\bigr)
\subset \mathbb{P}^4,

where [x_0 : x_1 : x_2 : x_3 : x_4] are homogeneous coordinates.

The non-commutative coordinate ring of \mathcal{B} is the quotient

\mathcal{O}_q(\mathcal{B})
=  \mathcal{O}_q(\mathbb{P}^4) \big/
\bigl(
  \textstyle\sum x_i,
  \textstyle\sum x_i^2,
  \textstyle\sum x_i^3
\bigr),

where \mathcal{O}_q(\mathbb{P}^4) is the quantum polynomial ring with relations x_i x_j = q x_j x_i for i < j.
rem:brings-coordinate-ring-remark:
Remark Genus, S_5-symmetry and the Reeb spectrum of Bring's curve. Bring's curve \mathcal{B} is a smooth algebraic curve of genus g = 4; it serves as the spectral coordinate fibre of the algebraic layer.

The symmetric group S_5 acts on \mathcal{B} by permutation of the homogeneous coordinates. This action descends to an S_5-action on \mathcal{O}_q(\mathcal{B}) by algebra automorphisms, realizing the five-fold combinatorial symmetry of the aether. The 2g = 8 fundamental modes of the Reeb spectrum correspond to the 8 independent cycles of \mathcal{B}, providing the spectral basis for the derivation \xi_q.
ex:categorical-reeb-brings: Example Constructive Reeb derivation on Bring's coordinate ring. On the Bring coordinate ring \mathcal{O}_q(\mathcal{B}), the categorical Reeb derivation is constructed explicitly. The generator in \mathfrak{su}(2) is \xi = e_3. On A = \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)), \xi acts as the infinitesimal adjoint coaction, acting diagonally on the standard generators. This action defines a derivation. The dual form \varTheta_A = \omega_3 is the left-invariant basis element from Woronowicz's three-dimensional left-covariant differential calculus [woronowicz1987-twisted-su2, woronowicz1989]. Normalization holds by definition: \omega_3(e_3) = 1. The contact identity \iota_\xi d\varTheta_A = 0 follows from the Woronowicz structure equations d\omega_3 = -q^{-1}\omega_+ \wedge \omega_-. The \xi-action extends S_5-equivariantly to the coordinates of Bring's curve. The 8 = 2g independent cycles split into eigenspaces of \xi with weights +1 and -1, precisely matching the fundamental modes.
def:aether-parameter-planck:
Definition Aether parameter and quantum Planck constant. The aether parameter q \in \mathbb{C}^* is the deformation parameter of the Frobenius--Hopf algebra A. The quantum Planck constant associated to q is

\hbar_q =  1 - q^{-1} =  \frac{q - 1}{q}.
